observation: The first combined round proposed sanitising every artifact body, including the `html` kind. Sanitising an html artifact strips the scripts that are the whole reason the kind exists, so the plan would have deleted the product feature while calling it a safety measure. The founder rejected it and the round was rewritten as an isolation decision split by kind. Nothing inside the pipeline caught it — the plan was internally coherent and read as thorough.

Three separate times a test was green while the thing it tested was broken. (1) The egress spec's only listener was a third-party origin, so every same-origin channel was invisible by construction and the `APP-API` assertion could not fail under any implementation. (2) The listener recorded `/META-REFRESH` while the assertion compared against `META-REFRESH`, so each per-channel check was unfalsifiable. (3) The bullet fix asserted a class name that Tailwind had never generated, so it was green in vitest and painted `list-style-type: none` on screen. None of the three was caught by the suite passing. Each was caught by deliberately removing the mitigation and watching whether the test went red, or by a fresh reader attacking the code.

Both real holes — self-navigation out of the frame, and `'self'` resolving to the app's own origin — were found by a reviewer who did not write the code, on a read-only pass, after the builder had declared the work done with green gates. The builder's own further testing found neither. The separation of producer and evaluator is what produced the findings, not the amount of testing.

`layers/core-ui/src/index.css:78` declares `@source "../../design-system/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"`, which resolves to `layers/design-system/` — a directory that does not exist; the design system is under `framework/`. So no utility class used only inside the design-system package has ever been generated. The practical consequence for testing: a class-name assertion on a design-system component can pass while the element paints wrong. Worked around here with an inline style plus lore; the glob itself is untouched because fixing it would apply every silently-dropped utility at once.

An e2e run silently reused a dev server left running by a sibling worktree on port 5179 — `playwright.config.ts` sets `reuseExistingServer` — and reported the pre-change DOM as if it were the current build. The run looked normal and the results were about other code. Every subsequent run in this work package checked `lsof` on 5179 first and started its own server.

The frame's CSP was adopted from the MCP Apps specification without re-reading each directive against our own architecture. MCP Apps serves frames from a host-controlled resource origin, where `'self'` is a narrow grant; ours is a `srcdoc` document with an opaque origin, where Chromium resolves `'self'` to the embedding app's origin. The borrowed shape was right and the borrowed tokens were wrong, and that alone cost the last two review rounds. The specific word matters less than the habit: a config taken from a spec whose threat model differs from yours has to be re-derived line by line.

The caption under the frame went through three wordings across the rounds, each one an absolute promise about what the artifact could not do, and each one falsified by the next review. It now says what the frame is — it runs on its own, in a box sealed off from the app — which is a sentence whose truth does not depend on having enumerated every channel in the web platform. The founder's ruling that settled it: nothing escapes is impossible in IT, and this is an MVP.

This work package ran the founder-approved short procedure — one combined refine+design+architecture round, one build session, one review — and then took three review rounds anyway, all three on the isolation decision rather than on the rendering work the work package was actually about. The rendering half was right on the first build and was never contested.

A defence was built for a case that could not occur and was cut on review. `ArtifactFrame` counted load events on the shell iframe and painted a 'tried to leave its box' panel on a second one, guarding against the shell being replaced — which nothing in an artifact can cause. The argument that settled it came from the code itself, not from new measurement: the *Open larger* dialog rendered the identical srcDoc in a second iframe with no counter, so if the threat were real the largest view of the artifact was the unguarded one. Either it matters everywhere or it matters nowhere. Written under review pressure after two rounds of found holes, it was reflex rather than reasoning. The lore explaining why no backstop is needed was kept and is worth more than the backstop was.
